content: 1. Antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis should be administered as appropriate for wounds that are potentially contaminated. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended several post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimens, which vary based on clinical care settings and country-specific preferences. These regimens have been evaluated for immunogenicity, clinical outcomes, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness. 3. WHO recognizes the clinical equivalence of the intradermal route for PEP administration. Intradermal administration is preferred in clinics that manage multiple new bite patients weekly, as it is the most cost-effective method. 4. Rabies vaccines labeled for intramuscular use can be safely administered intradermally, even if this constitutes off-label use. 5. For adults, the rabies vaccine should always be injected into the deltoid area of the arm. For children under two years of age, the anterolateral area of the thigh is recommended. 6. A single intramuscular dose of rabies vaccine consists of an entire vial, regardless of the vial size. For intradermal administration, 1 mL of vaccine is used, accounting for dead space in the syringe or needle mount. 7. Rabies vaccines and rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) can be safely used during pregnancy and lactation. Life-saving PEP should never be withheld from pregnant or lactating women, and any WHO-recommended PEP regimen can be utilized. 8. WHO-recommended PEP regimens include intradermal and intramuscular schedules, with variations in duration and injection sites. Alternative immunogenic intradermal regimens are also available for specific circumstances. 9. Intradermal rabies PEP regimens can be shortened without compromising clinical outcomes, as demonstrated in studies conducted in Cambodia. 10. In unavoidable circumstances, changes in the rabies vaccine product or administration route are permissible to ensure the completion of a PEP schedule. Restarting PEP is not necessary; the new administration route's schedule should be adopted. 11. For immunocompromised individuals, meticulous wound cleaning is critical. When feasible, the rabies virus-neutralizing antibody response should be measured 2–4 weeks after vaccination to determine if an additional vaccine dose is required. 12. Immunocompromised patients, including those with HIV under treatment, generally respond to rabies vaccines similarly to healthy individuals. However, the most immunogenic PEP options, including high-quality vaccines and RIG, should be prioritized. 13. For previously immunized individuals exposed or re-exposed to rabies, RIG is not indicated. Simplified PEP regimens, such as intradermal or intramuscular vaccine administration on specific days, can be used. 14. If prior PEP or pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) cannot be documented, a full PEP regimen, including RIG if indicated, should be administered. 15. RIG provides neutralizing antibodies at the exposure site before the patient produces their own antibodies. It should be administered only once, preferably at the start of PEP, and is not indicated beyond the seventh day after the first vaccine dose. 16. The maximum dose of human RIG is 20 IU/kg of body weight, while equine immunoglobulin and F(ab')2 products have a maximum dose of 40 IU/kg. The entire dose should be infiltrated into or near the wound(s) as anatomically feasible. 17. Injecting the remaining RIG volume intramuscularly at a distance from the wound provides little additional protection compared to wound infiltration alone. 18. In cases of mucosal exposure without a wound, rinsing with RIG can be considered. For suspected aerosol exposure to rabies virus, intramuscular RIG injection is recommended. 19. Mixing rabies vaccine and RIG in the same syringe or using the same syringe for both is not advised. 20. For severe or multiple wounds requiring more RIG than the maximum dose, the product may be diluted with sterile saline to ensure effective infiltration of all wounds. 21. Monoclonal antibody (mAb) products, licensed in India in 2017, are being used as alternatives to RIG in clinical settings, depending on geographical and epidemiological contexts. 22. There are no contraindications to PEP, and it can be safely administered to infants, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals, including children with HIV/AIDS. 23. PEP should be administered by adequately trained staff in settings where adverse reactions can be managed. Recipients should be observed for at least 15–20 minutes after vaccination. 24. If a patient has a known allergy to a rabies vaccine component, an alternative vaccine product should be used for PrEP or PEP. 25. Governments and responsible agencies should ensure timely access to adequate PEP for all individuals with suspected, probable, or confirmed rabies exposure. Intradermal administration should be included in national recommendations. 26. In settings with limited vaccine or RIG supplies, prioritization should be given to high-risk exposures, such as multiple or deep bites, bites to highly innervated areas, or bites from animals with confirmed or probable rabies. 27. Travelers to rabies-affected areas should assess their risk of exposure based on the remoteness of the destination, local rabies epidemiology, and the duration of their stay. 28. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) should be considered for individuals engaging in activities with a high risk of rabies exposure, such as caving or extensive outdoor activities in remote areas. 29. Travelers should avoid contact with free-roaming animals, especially dogs, cats, and monkeys, as well as wild animals. Cavers should be warned not to handle bats. 30. Education programs to prevent dog bites are essential for reducing rabies risk, minimizing PEP costs, and fostering healthy human-dog relationships. These programs are most effective when they involve live dogs and address the complex interaction of knowledge, emotion, and experience. 31. Surveys on knowledge, attitudes, and practices should guide the development of rabies education programs. Bite prevention education may also include guidance on avoiding contact with wildlife in rabies-endemic areas.
